notes: Long TCC defects trial; draft judgment on retention, certificates and set-off is detailed though parties settled after receipt.

enrichment.short_title: Birse v ET: JCT retention, making-good certificates and construction defects
key_facts: Birse built a high-specification Cable and Wireless training college in Coventry under a JCT 1980 contract with MacCormac Jamieson Prichard as architect.
Practical completion was certified in December 1993 but extensive snagging and later defects led to disputes over retention and remedial works.
Birse claimed release of retention and further sums; ET counterclaimed for remedied and unremedied defects totalling about £1.5 million.
A March 1994 agreement sought to bring finality to listed snagging defects but did not resolve the wider defects dispute.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of Birse's claim for retention and final account sums against ET's abatement, set-off and counterclaim for construction defects.
enrichment.outcome: The judge held Birse liable for many outstanding defects, ET could not rely on the absence of a certificate of making good defects to defeat Birse's claim, nominal damages of £2 were awarded to ET, and the parties settled after receipt of the draft judgment.
enrichment.ratio: Where works remain below the contractual standard no certificate of making good defects can properly be issued and the employer cannot treat continuing non-certification as a complete defence to the contractor's retention claim; the employer retains abatement, set-off and counterclaim rights, and an architect's exacting aesthetic standards under the contract must be respected unless unreasonable.
legal_issues: Whether release of retention under clause 4 depended on certificates of making good defects
Construction and effect of the March 1994 snagging agreement
Extent of Birse's liability for remedied and unremedied defects
Whether ET's intention to sell the college affected recoverable damages

confidence.notes: Core holdings on certificates, retention and liability are clearly stated though quantum was settled after the draft judgment.

notes: Case stated appeal on PACE entry and breach-of-peace arrest; Fulford J's analysis is straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Blench v DPP: PACE section 17 entry and assault on arresting officer
key_facts: Police attended Mr Blench's home after a 999 call reporting a drunken man trying to remove a child.
Mr Blench aggressively ordered officers off the property and obstructed their attempted entry to check on children inside.
Officers entered under section 17(1)(e) PACE, used CS spray, arrested him for breach of the peace and he spat at PC Parsons during detention.
Justices convicted him of assaulting a police constable in the execution of his duty.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' conviction for assault on a police constable in execution of duty.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; there was evidence to reject no case to answer, section 17(1)(e) entitled officers to enter, the arrest was lawful and PC Parsons was acting in execution of his duty when assaulted.
enrichment.ratio: Section 17(1)(e) PACE provides a complete answer to a trespass challenge where officers enter to save life or limb after a worrying emergency call; aggressive conduct and obstruction can found breach of the peace and lawful arrest, and delayed formal arrest for assault does not retrospectively invalidate lawful detention for breach of the peace.
legal_issues: Whether there was evidence of breach of the peace before arrest
Whether police became trespassers after the occupier revoked permission to remain
Whether officers were entitled to enter under section 17(1)(e) PACE
Whether PC Parsons was acting in execution of his duty when spat at
linked_authorities: R (on the application of Laporte) v Chief Constable of Gloucestershire [2004] 2 All ER 874
Lesley Edward Bibby v Chief Constable of Essex Police (2000) 164 JP 297

confidence.notes: Chronological fact analysis and answers to the four stated questions are explicit.

notes: Short agreed SEN judicial review; school naming issue became academic on move to Lincolnshire.

enrichment.short_title: R(O) v Wiltshire: remittal on hydrotherapy in special educational needs statement
key_facts: The claimant's son T has severe microcephaly, spastic diplegia and profound learning difficulties.
Parents challenged a Special Educational Needs Tribunal decision upholding Wiltshire's maintained-school placement rather than a residential non-maintained school.
The family was imminently moving to Lincolnshire, making the Part 4 school dispute academic.
The tribunal had not addressed hydrotherapy and associated facilities in Part 3 of the statement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Special Educational Needs Tribunal decision on a statement of special educational needs.
enrichment.outcome: Parties agreed to remit the hydrotherapy issue to a fresh tribunal; time to serve the appeal was extended and there was no order as to costs save Legal Services Commission assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Where a child is moving local authority the identity of the named school may become academic, but unresolved Part 3 provision such as hydrotherapy still requires tribunal determination because the existing statement transfers to the new authority until reassessment.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal properly named the maintained school in Part 4
Whether hydrotherapy provision required remittal
Effect of the family's move to Lincolnshire on the appeal
Whether time to serve the claim should be extended

confidence.notes: Agreed remittal order and reasoning on continuing Part 3 issues are clear though the judgment is brief.

notes: Working Time Regulations airport-catering appeal; Peter Gibson LJ's construction analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Gallagher v Alpha Catering: Regulation 21(c) rest breaks for airport loaders
key_facts: Twenty-eight Alpha Flight Services employees at Gatwick claimed unlawful denial of 20-minute rest breaks under regulation 12.
Their work involved time-critical aircraft loading and de-catering with substantial downtime waiting at the airport under radio contact.
An employment tribunal held regulation 21(c) excluded them because continuity of service was needed at airports.
The EAT allowed the employees' appeal, holding the derogation focused on the worker's activities not the employer's business.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on Working Time Regulations rest-break derogations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on regulation 21(c); permission refused on regulation 21(d), downtime and regulation 24 points.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 21(c) excludes rest breaks only where the individual worker's activities involve the need for continuity of service or production; an employer's time-critical airport operation does not automatically bring every worker within the derogation, and downtime while on call at the employer's disposal is not a rest break.
legal_issues: Whether regulation 21(c) refers to worker or employer activities
Whether routine daily and weekly fluctuations amounted to a foreseeable surge under regulation 21(d)
Whether downtime of 20 minutes or more qualified as a rest break
Whether compensatory rest under regulation 24 remained in issue
linked_authorities: Bowden v Tuffnells Parcels Express Ltd [2001] IRLR 838
SIMAP v Conselleria de Sanidad y Consumo de la Generalidad Valenciana [2000] IRLR 845

confidence.notes: Central statutory construction issue and dismissal are clearly reasoned across multiple regulation points.

notes: Section 34 adverse-inference appeal; unsafe conviction findings are detailed despite absent transcript.

enrichment.short_title: R v C: unsafe conviction from defective section 34 summing-up

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: A 17-year-old with literacy difficulties was convicted of indecent assault at a gym after giving a prepared police statement and 'no comment' answers on advice.
At trial he said the complainant had propositioned him and he declined because his wife was pregnant.
The judge gave a formulaic section 34 direction without identifying the specific fact omitted at interview.
The judge also commented adversely on defence evidence including the complainant's acting and family witnesses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited appeal with leave against conviction for indecent assault in the Crown Court at Luton.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and conviction quashed as unsafe; prosecution did not seek retrial.
enrichment.ratio: A section 34 adverse inference direction must identify the specific fact subsequently relied on and be tailored to the case; a generic JSB formula is fatal where the only omitted detail was conversation content after a prepared denial, especially for a young, unsophisticated defendant advised to remain silent.
legal_issues: Whether the section 34 direction identified facts the defendant failed to mention
Whether the JSB specimen direction was appropriate on these facts
Whether adverse inference should have been given to a 17-year-old advised by a solicitor
Whether the judge's summing-up was fair overall
linked_authorities: R v Turner [2004] 1 Cr App R 24

confidence.notes: Primary ground on section 34 misdirection is fully reasoned though some subsidiary summing-up points rest on solicitor's notes.

notes: Vexatious litigant renewed permission application; general civil restraint order clearly granted.

enrichment.short_title: Kumar v SoS Constitutional Affairs: general civil restraint order for vexatious claims
key_facts: Mr Kumar, appearing in person, sought judicial review of High Court district registry decisions and to stop a November 2004 hearing.
Munby J had refused permission on the papers as an abuse of process.
The applicant had a history of numerous unmeritorious claims against government departments and universities.
The Secretary of State applied for a civil restraint order under Bhamjee principles.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed oral application for permission to apply for judicial review, with an application for a general or extended civil restraint order.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; a general civil restraint order for up to two years was made prohibiting new High Court or county court proceedings without permission of Moses J or Collins J.
enrichment.ratio: Judicial review is not the route to challenge county court or High Court registry decisions, which lie by appeal to the Court of Appeal; persistent meritless litigation causing disproportionate harassment warrants a general civil restraint order rather than a narrower extended order.
legal_issues: Whether registry decisions could be challenged by judicial review
Whether Convention rights provided a new basis for permission
Whether an extended or general civil restraint order was appropriate
Whether the applicant's litigation history showed vexatious persistence
linked_authorities: Bhamjee v Forsdick & Ors [2003] EWCA Civ 1113
Kumar v Lord Chancellor's Department [2004] EWHC 654

confidence.notes: Permission refusal and two-year general restraint order are stated plainly with supporting litigation history.

notes: Section 288 Green Belt gypsy site challenge; Sullivan J's very-special-circumstances analysis is authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: Basildon v Temple: Green Belt gypsy site and very special circumstances
key_facts: An inspector granted retrospective planning permission for a single-family gypsy caravan site at Hatchertang in the Metropolitan Green Belt at Wickford.
Basildon District Council refused permission and challenged the decision under section 288.
The inspector found a severe shortage of alternative gypsy accommodation and significant hardship to the Temple family if the appeal failed.
The site was relatively small and self-contained though inappropriate development in the Green Belt.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to a planning inspector's decision granting retrospective permission for change of use to a gypsy caravan site.
enrichment.outcome: Challenge dismissed on both grounds; the council must pay the Secretary of State's costs summarily assessed at £3,820.
enrichment.ratio: Very special circumstances for Green Belt inappropriate development may arise from a combination of ordinary factors rather than each factor individually being very special; an inspector may properly weigh gypsy site shortage, family hardship and educational continuity against limited Green Belt harm.
legal_issues: Whether very special circumstances must each individually be 'very special'
Whether the inspector correctly balanced Green Belt harm against gypsy accommodation need
Whether the inspector erred on alternative bricks-and-mortar accommodation
Whether winter horse stabling was adequately considered
index_terms: Chelmsford Borough Council v First Secretary of State
linked_authorities: Basildon District Council v Secretary of State for the Environment [2001] JPL 1104
Chelmsford Borough Council v First Secretary of State [2003] EWHC 2978 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Both grounds of challenge are addressed in detail with clear dismissal and costs order.

notes: Commercial LOI and third-party rights preliminary issues; Cooke J's 1999 Act analysis is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Laemthong Glory: letters of indemnity and third-party enforcement
key_facts: Sugar cargo was discharged at Aden against charterers' and receivers' letters of indemnity without production of bills of lading.
The Yemen and Kuwait Bank arrested the vessel claiming misdelivery after retaining the bills under a letter of credit dispute.
Owners sought orders that charterers and receivers provide bail under clause 3 of the indemnities.
Receivers argued the indemnity chain and 1999 Act presumptions prevented direct enforcement by owners.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of preliminary issues on construction and enforceability of letters of indemnity and entitlement to specific performance of security obligations.
enrichment.outcome: Owners may enforce both the charterers' and receivers' letters of indemnity; specific performance of clause 3 bail obligations was appropriate though release of the vessel was imminent.
enrichment.ratio: A receivers' letter of indemnity addressed to charterers but requiring delivery through the owners' agents purports to confer a benefit on owners enforceable under the 1999 Act; clause 3 bail obligations are not merely secondary damages remedies but primary obligations warranting specific performance to secure release of the arrested vessel.
legal_issues: Whether owners were 'agents' of charterers within the receivers' indemnity
Whether section 1(1)(b) of the 1999 Act applied to clauses 1 and 3
Whether the parties rebutted third-party enforceability by an indemnity chain
Whether damages were an adequate remedy or specific performance should issue
linked_authorities: Nisshin Shipping Co Ltd v Cleaves & Co Ltd [2004] 1 Lloyd's Rep 38

confidence.notes: Preliminary issue disposals on construction, third-party rights and specific performance are explicit.

notes: Complex mental-health/community-care consent-order dispute; applications adjourned for further directions.

enrichment.short_title: Hickmott v Brighton: Beaconsfield Villas consent order and mental health placement
key_facts: The claimant with learning disability, autism and epilepsy was detained under section 3 at a private hospital.
A September 2002 consent order required Brighton and Hove Council to implement a placement at Beaconsfield Villas.
The council later sought discharge of the consent order saying the unit was no longer suitable and clinicians disagreed on placement.
The claimant sought enforcement while the council argued changed circumstances and consensus among some doctors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review applications concerning discharge or enforcement of a consent order settling earlier community-care proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: The council failed to establish discharge of the September 2002 consent order and the claimant did not establish that it should remain enforced; both applications were adjourned with detailed directions for further medical and planning evidence.
enrichment.ratio: A consent order settling community-care litigation should not be discharged without sufficiently clear evidence addressing changed circumstances; where responsible clinicians diverge on whether a planned placement remains appropriate, the court should adjourn and require focused evidence rather than grant discharge on an unclear consensus view.
legal_issues: Whether the September 2002 consent order should be discharged for changed circumstances
Whether the claimant was entitled to enforcement of the Beaconsfield Villas project
Whether the claimant required hospital registration or dual registration for lawful treatment
Whether section 17 leave or declaratory relief could resolve treatment disputes

confidence.notes: Interim conclusions and adjournment directions are clear though final placement outcome was not determined.

notes: Patent case-management application; Pumfrey J's four-bit order enforced by HHJ Fysh.

enrichment.short_title: Halliburton v Smith: case management of drill-bit disclosure selection
key_facts: Halliburton sued Smith for infringement of two drill-bit patents after winning a related US jury trial.
Proceedings began in the Patents County Court but were transferred to the High Court with revocation counterclaims.
Smith produced a detailed product and process description and a list of 134 imported drill bits.
Pumfrey J ordered each side to select four exemplar drill bits rather than full disclosure on all listed products.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application to enforce Pumfrey J's disclosure order requiring Halliburton to nominate four exemplar drill bits for trial.
enrichment.outcome: Halliburton's application for full disclosure on all listed bits was refused; it was ordered to nominate four drill bits by 6pm on 9 November and inspection was fixed for 15-19 November.
enrichment.ratio: Where a patent defendant has provided a comprehensive product and process description and a complete import list, the court may limit disclosure to selected exemplar products rather than permit fishing through every potentially infringing article, especially where the claimant already has extensive US discovery and expert knowledge.
legal_issues: Whether Halliburton should be required to select four exemplar drill bits
Whether full disclosure of all 151 listed imported bits was necessary
Whether Pumfrey J's case-management order should be reopened
Timing of inspection following nomination

confidence.notes: Interlocutory orders and reasoning on limiting disclosure are clearly recorded though merits of infringement were not decided.
